title: Visual Self-Refine: A Pixel-Guided Paradigm for Accurate Chart Parsing
one_liner: ChartVSR asks the model to mark the exact chart pixels for each data point, feeds those markings back as an image, and refines them before decoding the final table, so visual errors are corrected in the image space where they arise.
lead: Chart parsing means turning a chart image into structured values such as categories, series names, and numeric coordinates. Large vision-language models reason well in text, but dense charts fail for a simpler reason: the model first misreads where a bar end, line marker, or axis tick actually sits. Once that visual mistake is made, later text reasoning only rearranges wrong evidence. Visual Self-Refine changes the loop. The model first predicts pixel localizations, meaning explicit image positions for data points or chart elements, then renders those predictions back into the image and inspects them again. Refinement happens on the visual evidence itself rather than only on the text answer.

problem.h2: Why dense charts defeat text-only self-correction
paras: A chart answer depends on accurate visual grounding. If the model reads the wrong bar top, confuses two nearby line points, or misses a legend color, the final parsed table is already wrong before any language reasoning begins. Dense plots make this common because many marks are visually close and small shifts in pixel position can change a value materially.

Standard self-correction for language models revises text after the model sees its previous answer. That helps when the error is logical or verbal. It does much less when the error is a misplaced pixel coordinate, because the model is still revising from the same hidden visual guess rather than from a checked visual anchor.

callout.html: Predict pixel locations first, draw them back onto the chart, refine those locations iteratively, and only then decode the structured values, so the final parser reads from verified visual anchors instead of from an unchecked first guess.

panels.title: 1. Dense chart, many close marks
panels.viz_args: bars, lines, ticks, legend colors, labels
panels.caption: Several visual cues must be read jointly, and each can sit only a few pixels from a distractor.

panels.title: 2. First pass misses a point
panels.caption: A small localization error changes the mapped value or connects the wrong series.

panels.title: 3. Draw predicted anchors back on the chart
panels.caption: The model sees its own marks as visible overlays in the image.

panels.title: 4. Refine the marked pixels
panels.viz_args: shift point up 3 px | reassign legend color | add missing marker
panels.caption: The second pass corrects omissions and misalignments by inspecting the overlaid anchors.

panels.title: 5. Decode the final table
panels.caption: The parser converts checked pixel anchors into structured chart data.

steps.text: For each relevant chart element, output image coordinates or regions rather than jumping directly to final values.
Render those predicted points, boxes, or traces onto the chart image because the overlay exposes the exact places chosen by the earlier pass.
Ask the model to adjust missed, duplicated, or shifted anchors after seeing the overlaid image, which exposes visual mistakes directly.
Once the localized points are stable, treat them as trusted inputs for the decoding stage rather than allowing new free-form visual guesses.
Map the checked anchors through the axes, legends, and labels to produce final numeric values and series assignments.

paras: The paper changes the intermediate object passed between perception and reasoning. Instead of handing the decoder an uninspected hidden visual state, it hands over explicit pixel anchors that the model has already seen, drawn, and refined.

hidden.name: localization reliability (whether the predicted pixel anchor truly sits on the intended chart mark)
paras: The hidden quantity is not the final chart value but the trustworthiness of the predicted anchor location. A bar chart value becomes wrong if the anchor is even a few pixels off the true bar end. A line chart series becomes wrong if one marker is assigned to the neighboring series.

Visual Self-Refine measures this reliability indirectly by closing the loop through the image. When the model redraws its predicted anchors and looks again, missing points, overlap conflicts, and offset markers become visible in the same modality where the mistake occurred. That is why the refinement stage can fix perception errors that text-only revision leaves untouched.

heat.caption: The darker cells are the visual cues whose pixel placement most strongly determines whether the decoded chart table will be correct.

reads.html: Before asking what number a point means, the model must verify that the point it selected is actually the right mark in the image.
The refine stage iteratively validates pixel-level localizations through visual feedback, and the decode stage then treats those localizations as anchors for structured parsing.

paras: The method works because chart parsing has a hard dependency chain. Values come from positions, positions come from marks, and marks must be correctly separated from nearby distractors. If the first link is wrong, later reasoning cannot repair it reliably. Visual Self-Refine attacks the earliest failure point by making localization an explicit object that can be checked.

Feeding the overlay back to the model changes the evidence available on the next pass. The model no longer relies only on an internal memory of where it pointed. It sees the chart together with its own chosen anchors, so it can notice direct visual mismatches such as an anchor floating above a bar top or sitting on the wrong color trace. After refinement, the decode stage becomes simpler because it reads from anchored coordinates instead of from a vague hidden guess.

stages.s: chart image with bars, lines, labels, and legend
predict explicit pixel anchors for chart elements
render anchors back onto the chart image
refine anchor locations iteratively until stable
decode values and series identity from the verified anchors
structured chart table with fewer omissions and misalignments

math.words: Training combines a localization loss on predicted anchor positions with a decoding loss on the final chart table, so the model is rewarded both for pointing to the right pixels and for producing the right parsed output.
symbols: loss on the predicted pixel locations or regions for chart elements
loss on the decoded structured chart output after the refine stage
weight that balances final parsing accuracy against raw localization accuracy

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a predicted line marker is 4 pixels away from the labeled target point, giving L_loc = 0.12 after normalization.
The decoded value from that point is also off, giving L_dec = 0.20.
If lambda_dec = 2, then the total is 0.12 + 2 * 0.20 = 0.52.
That weighting tells training that an anchor is not good enough just because it is close in pixels. It must also support the correct parsed value after refinement.

math.note: The two losses cooperate because chart parsing needs correct positions before it can produce correct values.

charts.title: Direct chart parsing without visual refinement
charts.note: The model answers from an unchecked visual guess, so local perception mistakes propagate into the final table.

charts.title: ChartVSR with refine then decode
charts.note: Explicit anchor refinement reduces the perception errors first, so the later decode stage reads cleaner evidence.

items.b: The initial anchors are too far off.
items.html: Refinement assumes the model marks roughly relevant regions first. If the first pass lands on unrelated chart parts, the feedback loop can reinforce the wrong structure instead of correcting it.

Very dense charts with many predicted anchors can make the feedback image hard to read, which reduces the benefit of the second pass because the model now has to parse the chart and the overlay simultaneously.
Even with correct anchor pixels, the final value can stay wrong if the axes are logarithmic, truncated, or labeled in an unusual way and the decode stage does not model that convention well.

The approach is strongest when anchors are close enough for visual feedback to expose the remaining errors and when the decode stage can reliably map checked positions through the chart axes and legend.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a benchmark of bar charts and line charts where nearby points, dense legends, and small axis spacing cause common parsing errors. Run a baseline that decodes directly from the image and a two-stage system that predicts anchors, overlays them, refines them, and then decodes. Save the intermediate overlay images for manual inspection.

The demo should make the main mechanism visible: final chart accuracy should rise when the intermediate anchor images become cleaner, because the system is correcting the visual cause of the error before turning that evidence into values.
demo.metric_eq: point_error = mean absolute pixel distance between predicted anchors and labeled anchors
demo.closing: The most useful output is a pair of plots: anchor error before and after refinement, and final table accuracy before and after refinement. They should move together.
